name: Tropical dry forest
notes: Deciduous tropical forest with a long dry season: most trees drop leaves for 4-7 months, thorny/bottle-trunked species, open understory of shrubs and grasses. Drawn on Mesoamerican Pacific dry forest, Bolivian Chiquitano, Indian/Burmese dry deciduous forest, Miombo margins and Madagascar western dry forest.

canopy.name: Guanacaste
canopy.source: Enterolobium cyclocarpum, guanacaste/ear-pod tree, huge spreading crown in Pacific Central American dry forest, 20-35 m — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Enterolobium cyclocarpum, guanacaste/ear-pod tree, huge spreading crown in Pacific Central American dry forest, 20-35 m

canopy.silhouette: enormous low hemispherical dome, wider than tall

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal germination 3-7 days after the hard seed is scratched or passes through a horse or cow: two thick green cotyledons, then feathery bipinnate leaves. Grows as a fast single slender stem, often over 1 m in the first year, with an airy fern-like crown; branches low and spreads into the huge flat-topped umbrella only once well above the grass. Leafless in the dry season.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Enterolobium: scarified seed germinates in 3-7 days; pods take ~1 yr; 1000s of seeds/tree; 26-yr-old Puerto Rico plantation not yet flowering); Winrock/NFTA ear-pod tree factsheet (to 40 m; pod production delayed up to 25 yr); Wikipedia (25-35 m; seedlings >1 m in first year). Lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (flowers Mar-Apr on new leaves; ear-shaped legumes 7-12 cm, glossy dark brown, mature in ~a year and drop Mar-Apr); Winrock/NFTA (~2000 pods per tree, pods fall over ~2 months); Wikipedia (3 cm white fragrant heads, bee visitors, horses/cattle disperse; seeds eaten roasted). Fruit set and rot estimated.

canopy.name: Lignum vitae
canopy.origin: South Florida, Caribbean and Central America

bark.notes: mottled grey bark shedding in thin flakes

leaf.notes: opposite pinnate leaves of 2-5 pairs of small leathery obovate leaflets

flower.form: five-petalled blue-violet stars 1.5 cm in small clusters, fading paler

fruit.form: five-angled orange-yellow capsule that splits to show black seeds in scarlet arils

appearance.silhouette: dense dark dome of small leaves starred with blue flowers
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Little & Wadsworth 1964; Wikipedia Guaiacum sanctum

growth.juvenile_note: The seedling has two fleshy cotyledons then small opposite pinnate leaves; it grows extremely slowly (a few cm a year), becoming a twiggy, dense, dark-leaved sapling. Old trees are short, crooked-trunked and densely crowned.
growth.source: Little & Wadsworth 1964 (very slow growth, small tree to 10 m); Janzen 1983. Ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Little & Wadsworth 1964; Wikipedia (blue flowers in spring, yellow-orange 5-angled capsules splitting to show red-arillate seeds taken by birds). Counts estimated.

fruit.form: flat papery brown pods 6-12 cm with 1-3 seeds

appearance.seasonal: deciduous in the dry season, flowering bare
appearance.silhouette: open crown of pinnate leaves, bare and podded in the dry season
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Janzen 1983; Wikipedia Dalbergia retusa

growth.juvenile_note: Winged seed in a flat pod germinates with the rains; the seedling is a thin whip with small pinnate leaves that drops them in its first dry season. It grows slowly into a crooked-boled tree with a spreading open crown.
growth.source: Janzen 1983 Costa Rican Natural History; CITES/Tropicos notes on Dalbergia retusa (slow-growing, 20 m). Ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Janzen 1983 (flowers on the leafless crown in the dry season, bee-pollinated; flat wind-dispersed pods). Counts estimated.

canopy.name: Pochote

bark.notes: smooth grey-green trunk studded with stout conical prickles

fruit.form: woody oblong capsule 10-15 cm splitting to release kapok floss

appearance.seasonal: deciduous through the dry season, flowering on bare branches
appearance.silhouette: spiny green-grey trunk under a flat open crown
appearance.refs: Gibbs & Semir 2003 Anales Jard. Bot. Madrid; Kew POWO

growth.source: Gibbs & Semir 2003 (tree 8-20 m, prickly trunk, flowers at night on the leafless crown, bat-pollinated); juvenile form by analogy with C. pentandra. Ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Gibbs & Semir 2003; Rzedowski 1978 (seeds toasted and eaten in Mexico). Counts estimated.

shrub.name: Coral bean
shrub.source: Erythrina berteroana, pito coral tree, thorny deciduous shrub/small tree of Central American dry forest, 4-8 m — Wikipedia

shrub.silhouette: small thorny tree with red flower spikes

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal germination from the scarlet seed: two thick fleshy cotyledons, then trifoliate leaves with broad rhombic leaflets on a fast, thick, green, sparsely prickly single stem that often branches low. Most plants in the landscape are living fence posts: thick cuttings that root and leaf out within weeks and flower in 1-2 years.
growth.source: USDA Tropical Tree Seed Manual (Erythrina berteroana: tree to 12-15 m; 85-90% germination; living fenceposts; 30-50 pods/tree); ICRAF Agroforestree database; Useful Tropical Plants. Growth curve and ages estimated from its fast living-fence growth.

fruiting.source: USDA Tropical Tree Seed Manual (flowers Dec-Mar, racemes to 0.5 m, narrow banner 8 x 2 cm, hummingbird-pollinated with 25% sugar nectar; pods to 30 x 1.5 cm ripen Feb-Apr; red seeds <10 mm; 30-50 pods/tree). Seeds toxic (Erythrina alkaloids); hang, rot, fruit set estimated.

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: thick blunt sausage branches, leaf tufts at tips

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two leafy cotyledons, then a single stout, soft, grey-green succulent stem crowned by a tuft of long oblong leaves with prominent parallel side veins. It does not branch until it first flowers (new shoots fork just below each flower cluster), so a young plant is a thick stick with a leaf tuft at the top. Leaves drop in the dry season; stems bleed white latex.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (3-3.6 m in 6 yr; cuttings flower in the first year; 5-8 m or more); Wikipedia (2-8 m, 7-8 m wide). Germination, time from seed to first flower (~2-3 yr) and lifespan estimated from grower reports.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (flowers 5-7.5 cm, 5 petals; hawkmoth pollination by deceit, little or no nectar; pods 17.5 cm with 20-60 winged seeds, rarely set); ICRAF (clusters of 50-60 flowers, some >200; flowering Jun-Nov, pods mature early spring; hard pointed pods to 18 cm, persistent). Colours, crop and decay estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two broad, leafy, rounded cotyledons on a thick, succulent green stem, then large, shallowly 3-5-lobed, heart-shaped leaves. The seedling is a single stout stem with a crown of big leaves and grows fast; after its first year it branches into a small, open, thick-twigged shrub-tree that drops its leaves in the dry season and bleeds clear latex when cut.
growth.source: Wikipedia (germination complete within 9 days, first yield 9-12 months, full after 2-3 yr, life expectancy ~40 yr, ~20 male flowers per female); ICRAF Agroforestree (up to 6 m, first fruit from 4-5 months, productive 40-50 yr).

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (terminal cymes, insect pollination, capsule 2.5-3 x 2-3 cm yellow then black, 90 days flower to ripe seed, 2-3 t seed/ha, flowers with the rains); Wikipedia (~20 male per female flower, phorbol-ester toxic seeds). Set and rot times estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds lie dormant about 6 months, then sprout with the rains: a narrow first blade, then a small tuft of soft, hairy leaves with a white midrib, slow for its first weeks while roots develop, then tillering fast. By the end of its first wet season it is a dense tussock of broad drooping leaves; later it sends up culms to 4 m with paired, feathery, silky racemes.
growth.source: Tropical Forages (seed dormant ~6 months after harvest; culms to 4 m; tussocks to 1 m wide; short-day, critical photoperiod 12-14 h; seed mature 32-44 d after flowering; needs full sun but tolerates light shade) and Wikipedia (to 4 m, tussocks ~70 cm; up to 244,000 seeds/yr, 65% viable, most within 5 m). Germination days, first-season flowering and lifespan estimated.

ground.name: Bromelia

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are small rosettes of narrow leaves already edged with hooked spines. They grow into big, fierce rosettes of long arching leaves with curved spines; at flowering the centre turns bright red. Each rosette flowers once and dies, but stolons build dense, impenetrable colonies.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Mexico, Central America, West Indies; planted as a spiny living fence; fruit used for gruel); bromeliad growers' data (seed germination 1-4 weeks; rosettes flower once then die); timings estimated. lifespan_years is the rosette.

repro.note: most bloom once then die, leaving pups; hummingbird-pollinated; tank species hold rainwater that frogs and insects breed in

They grow into a dense tussock of tall, coarse culms that turn rusty red as the loose, feathery panicles of paired, awned spikelets ripen at the end of the rains; burnt tussocks resprout from the base.
growth.source: Feedipedia (Hyparrhenia rufa: robust densely tufted perennial 60-240 cm, slow establishment ~6 months to 2 years, fast-growing once established, regrows after fire, no frost); germination, first seed and lifespan estimated.

It tolerates the shade of savanna trees better than most grasses.

epiphyte.name: Dry-forest orchid
epiphyte.source: Encyclia cordigera, epiphytic orchid characteristic of Mesoamerican Pacific dry forest — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Encyclia cordigera, epiphytic orchid characteristic of Mesoamerican Pacific dry forest — Wikipedia

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-like seed germinates with a fungal partner into a tiny green protocorm on bark or rock; within months it roots and puts up a first strap leaf. The young plant is a small clump of egg-shaped green pseudobulbs, each topped by two or three stiff, leathery strap leaves, adding one bulb a year until it flowers on tall spikes of brown-petalled, pink-lipped fragrant flowers.

epiphyte.name: Leopard orchid

growth.juvenile_note: Starts as a dust-like seed that must meet a fungus; it swells into a tiny green protocorm on bark, then a thread of roots and one or two narrow strap leaves. Over years it builds a clump of upright, yellow, cane-like pseudobulbs (to 60 cm) with 6-7 pleated strap leaves near the top, ringed by a basket of stiff, upward-pointing white aerial roots that trap leaf litter.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Ansellia africana: robust clumps, some estimated over a tonne; yellow cane-like pseudobulbs to 60 cm with 6-7 leathery plicate leaves; upward-pointing white aerial roots forming a litter basket; panicles to 85 cm with 10-100 fragrant flowers 6 cm across, each lasting up to ~10 days). Germination, growth and ages estimated from orchid biology.

repro.note: dust seed by wind; germinates only where its fungus lives (reads mycorrhizal presence); most species need one specific pollinator

growth.juvenile_note: From a spore a green protonema on bark buds creeping shoots with flattened shiny leaves; the mat spreads a centimetre or two a year and sends up red-brown capsules on stalks 1-2 cm long.
growth.source: Buck 1998 (Entodon macropodus: on bark and rock, widespread in the tropics); growth and ages estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.name: Palm ruffle lichen
epiphyte.source: Parmotrema tinctorum (Despr. ex Nyl.) Hale, palm ruffle lichen, a large foliose lichen of sunny bark and rock in the tropics and subtropics, rosettes to 20 cm (Index Fungorum; Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff 2001 Lichens of North America; Hale 1965)
epiphyte.silhouette: broad pale grey leafy rosettes on sunny bark

leaf.notes: broad rounded mineral-grey lobes 1-2 cm wide with crisped edges, upper surface dotted with isidia, black underside showing at the lifted rims; whole rosettes to 20 cm

appearance.silhouette: broad pale grey leafy rosettes on sunny bark
appearance.refs: Brodo et al. 2001 Lichens of North America; Index Fungorum

growth.juvenile_note: Starts from an isidium or soredium lodged in a bark crack: a pale grey dot that spreads outward as a ring of broad rounded lobes, adding a few millimetres a year, until it is a ruffled grey rosette a hand-span or more across.
growth.source: Brodo et al. 2001 (P. tinctorum: thallus to 20 cm, lobes 1-2 cm, isidiate, on bark and rock in warm regions); growth rate and ages estimated from foliose Parmeliaceae.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.name: Resurrection fern
epiphyte.source: Pleopeltis polypodioides, resurrection fern, drought-curling fern on rocks and trunks of Americas dry forest — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Pleopeltis polypodioides, resurrection fern, drought-curling fern on rocks and trunks of Americas dry forest — Wikipedia
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout on moss and bark of oak limbs into tiny heart-shaped prothalli; the first fronds are small, simple to shallowly lobed and leathery, then once-pinnatifid fronds with grey-scaly undersides. A slender creeping rhizome (about 2 mm thick) branches along the bark into a mat. In drought the fronds curl up grey-brown and look dead, turning green again within a day or two of rain.
growth.source: Wikipedia Pleopeltis polypodioides (fronds to 25 x 5 cm; rhizome 2 mm; survives losing up to 97% of its water and rehydrates in 24-48 h; spores summer to autumn; rhizome pieces root). Spore-to-plant time, growth and lifespan estimated from epiphytic Polypodiaceae.

epiphyte.note_habit: 1 Oct (Mike's play): an EPIPHYTE — a creeping mat of small leathery fronds on the upper side of big limbs, classically live oak, also cypress, other hardwoods and rock; never ground cover. 'Resurrection': in a dry spell the fronds curl and go grey-brown and can lose most of their water, then green and unfurl within hours of rain. The tropical dry forest copy had it in the ground tier, and as the first file loaded it set the tier for the whole game; all four copies now agree.

desiccation.source: Pleopeltis polypodioides: poikilohydric, desiccation-tolerant; in drought the fronds roll inward and show the grey-brown, densely scaled underside, and can lose up to ~97 % of their water; rehydrated by rain they flatten and turn green within hours, fully within about a day (USDA Forest Service / university extension accounts; Stuart 1968; Muslin & Homann 1992)
desiccation._note: Design 1 Oct §CD (Mike: it behaves as it does in real life). wet_rain_mm_h: local rain (WeatherSim.local_weather) at or above this counts as wetting. Dry: after curl_starts_game_h without rain the fronds begin to roll; by dry_after_game_days they are fully rolled (dry_curl 0-1) and dry_color with the scaly underside showing (dry_underside_shows). Rain: unfurling starts within unfurl_starts_game_h and the plant is flat and green by green_after_game_h. humidity_slows: fog and high humidity stretch the drying. dormant_when_dry: no growth while dry. First guesses on real timings; the designer tunes.
